meanings: to be willing to do sth
to be ready to do sth
to be happy to do sth

components.note: 乐 is the simplified form of 樂, which depicted a wooden 木 instrument strung with strings 幺, played with a pick 白 — music came to represent joy, giving 乐 its meaning 'happy, music.'
心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn lèyì bāngzhù nǐ.
example.english: I'm very willing to help you.
example.fact: 乐意 differs from the plainer 愿意 (also "willing") by carrying real gladness about the task — the 乐 ("happy") component means 乐意 signals eager warmth, not just bare consent, the way English sometimes distinguishes "I'd be happy to" from a flatter "I'm willing to."

components.note: 亻 (person) plus 乍 (suddenly/for the first time) — together suggesting a person making or doing something for the first time.

example.pinyin: Zhè zhǒng yào de zuòyòng shì zhǐtòng.
example.english: This medicine's function is to relieve pain.
example.fact: 作用 rarely stands alone as a full verb meaning "to act upon"; it usually appears inside the fixed collocation 起作用 ("to take effect," literally "to rise up into function") whenever Chinese needs to say that something is having an effect.

components.note: 月 (moon) — 期 relates to time measured by the moon's cycles, like a period or term.
其 (qí) gives a hint of the sound — 期 is pronounced qī, a connection that has shifted slightly in tone.
彳 (a road/step) — someone arriving on the road
寺 (a court/hall) — the destination where the visitor is welcomed

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn qīdài zhè cì lǚxíng.
example.english: I'm really looking forward to this trip.
example.fact: 期待 sits at a slightly more formal, literary register than casual alternatives like 盼望 or the very colloquial 等不及 ("can't wait") — all three translate as "look forward to," but they don't sit at the same level of formality.

components.note: 八 (to divide/split) — represents something being separated into smaller parts.
亅 (a hook/line) — cutting a small piece off, an image tied to the meaning 'small, tiny.'
亻 (person) — 伙 relates to people who share meals or work together.
火 (huǒ) gives the sound — an exact match with 伙's reading huǒ.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.pinyin: Nàge xiǎohuǒzi hěn rèqíng.
example.english: That young man is very warm and friendly.
example.fact: 小伙子 is a colloquial term typically used by someone older to refer to a young man, rather than a label young men apply to themselves — its common feminine counterpart is 小姑娘 ("young girl, lass"), forming a matched informal pair.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 保 relates to a person looking after or protecting someone, originally a caretaker holding a child.
呆 (dāi) gives a hint of the sound — 保 is pronounced bǎo, a connection that has shifted over time.
阝 (hill) — 险 originally referred to steep, dangerous terrain
佥 (qiān) gives a sound distantly related to 险's reading xiǎn, having drifted apart over time

example.pinyin: Wǒ mǎile jiànkāng bǎoxiǎn.
example.english: I bought health insurance.
example.fact: 保险 covers both the financial-product sense ("insurance") and, unrelated in origin but identical in spelling, the everyday adjective sense of "safe, certain" — 这样做更保险 means "doing it this way is safer/surer," no policy involved.

components.note: 大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a human being.
一 (a line, here representing the sky) — drawn above a person, showing what is above them: the heavens, hence 'sky, day.'
亻 (person) — 使 involves a person carrying out a task.
吏 (a government official) — 使 originally referred to an official sent to carry out orders, giving rise to the meaning 'to make someone do something' or 'to use.'

example.pinyin: Tā de xiàoróng xiàng tiānshǐ yíyàng.
example.english: Her smile is like an angel's.
example.fact: 天使 is literally "heaven's messenger" (天 "heaven/sky" + 使 "envoy, messenger") — a fairly transparent calque coined to render the Christian concept of "angel" (from Greek angelos, itself "messenger") when it entered Chinese through missionary-era translation.

components.note: 又 (a hand) — reaching out to try to catch something.
隹 (a bird) — catching a bird by hand is hard, giving 难 its meaning 'difficult.'
罒 (a net) — 置 originally meant to set a net in place
直 (zhí) gives a sound close to 置's reading zhì, sharing a similar historical pronunciation

example.hanzi: 这个结果真是难以置信。
example.pinyin: Zhège jiéguǒ zhēnshì nányǐzhìxìn.
example.english: This result is truly hard to believe.
example.fact: 难以置信 is built from the productive prefix 难以 ("hard to") plus 置信 ("to place trust in") — the same 难以 combines with many other two-character verbs to form similar set phrases, such as 难以想象 ("hard to imagine") and 难以忍受 ("hard to bear").

components.note: 犭 (dog) — an old link behind 独's meaning 'alone, single, solitary'
虫 (chóng) gives a loose sound connection to 独's reading dú

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng dāndú gēn nǐ tántan.
example.english: I want to talk to you alone.
example.fact: 单独 describes how an action is carried out (单独 + verb, "to do something alone/separately") rather than an inner feeling of loneliness — for that emotional sense, Chinese reaches instead for 孤独, a common point of confusion since English "alone" covers both.

components.note: 阝 (a mound or place) — 队 pictures people gathering together.
人 (person) — people gathering in one place gave 队 its meaning 'a team' or 'a line/queue.'
长 (simplified from 長) depicts an elderly figure with long flowing hair and a cane — length and seniority are linked in the original picture.

example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒmen bān de duìzhǎng.
example.english: He is our class's team leader.
example.fact: 长 as a suffix meaning "head of ___" is highly productive and is always read zhǎng (never cháng "long") in this role — the same pattern behind 校长 ("principal"), 部长 ("minister"), and 组长 ("group leader").

components.note: 艹 (plant) — the original meaning of 著 related to plants standing out or being placed
者 (zhě) gives a sound close to one reading of 著, zhù; the common grammatical reading 'zhe' used here carries no stress and no clear tie to that sound
夕 (evening, night) — in the dark, one could not see a person's face, so calling out their name was necessary to identify them.
口 (mouth) — calling out with the mouth at night gave 名 its meaning 'name.'

example.pinyin: Zhè wèi zuòjiā hěn zhùmíng.
example.english: This author is very famous.
example.fact: 著名 leans toward a more literary, formal register — often describing scholars, works, or places — while its everyday synonym 有名 ("well-known") is the word more likely to come up describing a famous restaurant or a popular classmate.

components.note: 日 depicts the sun as a circle with a dot or short stroke inside — a simplified picture of the sun's disc, later squared off in the standard script.
木 (tree) — provides the base image of a tree.
一 (a line) marks the base of the trunk, highlighting the roots — giving 本 its meaning 'root, origin, source.'

example.pinyin: Tā míngnián yào qù Rìběn liúxué.
example.english: He wants to go study abroad in Japan next year.
example.fact: 日本 literally means "origin of the sun" (日 "sun" + 本 "root, origin") — a reference to Japan lying east of China, in the direction the sun rises, and the same logic behind the country's own native name, Nihon/Nippon.

components.note: 宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.

example.pinyin: Tā shì diànnǎo fāngmiàn de zhuānjiā.
example.english: He is an expert in computers.
example.fact: 专家 combines 专 ("specialized, focused") with the suffix 家, which marks a professional practitioner of a field — the same 家 that turns 作 ("to write") into 作家 ("writer") and 画 ("to paint") into 画家 ("painter").

components.note: 止 depicts a footprint, with toes at the top and the leg below — a simple picture of a foot, later extended to mean 'to stop.'

example.hanzi: 到目前为止,一切都很顺利。
example.pinyin: Dào mùqián wéizhǐ, yíqiè dōu hěn shùnlì.
example.english: So far, everything has gone smoothly.
example.fact: 为止 almost always closes a phrase opened by 到 (到...为止, "up until..."), most often in the fixed expression 到目前为止 ("up to now, so far") — it rarely appears on its own outside that frame.

components.note: 黑 (black) — 墨 describes something dark in color.
土 (earth) — black 黑 earth 土 gave 墨 its meaning 'ink,' a substance traditionally made from soot and clay-like binders.
西 is thought to depict a bird settling into its nest at dusk — since birds return to roost as the sun sets in the west, the character came to mean 'west.'
哥 doubles the character 可 ('to approve, to sing'), originally suggesting a call-and-response song between two singers; the meaning later narrowed to 'elder brother.'

example.pinyin: Tā de fùmǔ láizì Mòxīgē.
example.english: Her parents are from Mexico.
example.fact: 墨西哥 is a phonetic transliteration of "Mexico" — the characters were chosen purely to approximate the sound, so 墨 ("ink") contributes nothing to the meaning, unlike a calque such as 电脑 ("electric brain" = computer) where the characters' meanings actually build the concept.

components.note: 方 here depicts a flag or banner, marking a group on the move.
氏 depicts a person following behind — together, a group traveling together, giving 旅 its meaning 'trip, journey.'
饣 (food) points to a place where meals are served.
官 pictures an official hall or residence, giving 馆 its sense of a large public building.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen zài lǚguǎn zhùle sān tiān.
example.english: We stayed at the hotel for three days.
example.fact: 旅馆 is the older, more generic word for "hotel"; contemporary Mandarin, especially for nicer places, more often reaches for 宾馆 or the international-flavored 酒店, leaving 旅馆 to sound closer to a small, budget lodging house.

components.note: 心 (heart) — 恶 relates to an evil or malicious state of heart/mind
亚 (yà) gives a sound distantly related to 恶's reading è, having drifted apart over time

example.hanzi: 这个反派角色非常邪恶。
example.pinyin: Zhège fǎnpài juésè fēicháng xié'è.
example.english: This villain character is extremely evil.
example.fact: 邪恶 pairs 邪 ("deviant, unorthodox" — historically describing a straying from correct or orthodox belief and conduct, as in 邪教 "cult") with 恶 ("evil, vicious") — that first root still colors 邪恶 with a sense of corruption rather than plain cruelty.

components.note: 走 (to walk, to run) — 赶 relates to pursuing or hurrying, both forms of movement.
干 (gān) gives a rhyme close to gǎn, with the tone shifted.
忄 (heart/mind) — the state of mind being described.
夬 (a decisive, resolute action) — a resolute state of mind, giving 快 its meaning 'fast, quick.'

example.hanzi: 天要黑了,我们赶快回家吧。
example.pinyin: Tiān yào hēi le, wǒmen gǎnkuài huí jiā ba.
example.english: It's getting dark, let's hurry home.
example.fact: 赶快 usually appears as an urging directed at someone, often closing with 吧, rather than a neutral description of speed — to simply say an event happened quickly, Chinese instead reaches for 很快 or 迅速.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
口 (mouth) — 知 relates to speaking what one knows.
矢 (shǐ) gives a hint of the sound — 知 is pronounced zhī, a connection that has faded over time.

example.hanzi: 他不知这件事有多严重。
example.pinyin: Tā bùzhī zhè jiàn shì yǒu duō yánzhòng.
example.english: He didn't know how serious this matter was.
example.fact: 不知 is a terser, more written-register cousin of the everyday 不知道 — it drops the light suffix 道 and shows up mainly in formal writing and set phrases like 不知不觉 ("without realizing") and 不知所措 ("at a loss for what to do") rather than in casual speech.

components.note: 力 (strength) — 加 pictures adding one's effort to a cause.
口 (mouth, words) — combining strength with words of support gave 加 its meaning 'to add' or 'to increase.'

example.hanzi: 经过锻炼,他变得更加健康了。
example.pinyin: Jīngguò duànliàn, tā biànde gèngjiā jiànkāng le.
example.english: After exercising, he became even healthier.
example.fact: 更加 is a slightly more formal, two-syllable intensifier than the single-syllable 更 — both mean "even more," but 更加 turns up more in writing and speeches while 更 dominates everyday spoken comparisons like 更好 ("even better").

components.note: 女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'
几 depicts a small low table or stool with legs — a simple domestic object.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen děngle hǎojǐ gè xiǎoshí.
example.english: We waited for several hours.
example.fact: 好几 always precedes a measure word plus noun (好几个小时, 好几本书) and signals "a surprisingly large number of" — it sits closer to English "quite a few" than to a neutral "several," carrying a hint of the speaker's own surprise at the quantity.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 格 originally meant a wooden branch or standard, extended to 'pattern, style, rule.'
各 (gè) gives a sound hint — 格 is pronounced gé, sharing the same rhyme with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 这栋建筑的风格很独特。
example.pinyin: Zhè dòng jiànzhù de fēnggé hěn dútè.
example.english: This building's style is very unique.
example.fact: 风格 pairs 风 ("wind," extended metaphorically to "manner, prevailing trend," as in 风气 "atmosphere/practice" and 作风 "style of work") with 格 ("pattern, standard") — the drift from literal wind to "prevailing manner" echoes how English also describes a trend by "which way the wind is blowing."

components.note: 贝 (shell/money) — 费 relates to spending money, fees, and expenses
弗 (fú) gives a loose sound connection to 费's reading fèi

example.pinyin: Zhège huódòng shì miǎnfèi de.
example.english: This event is free.
example.fact: 免费 literally means "to exempt from a fee" (免 "to exempt, avoid" + 费 "fee, cost") and behaves as a verb-object compound — that's why it so often shows up directly before another verb, as in 免费入场 ("enter free of charge"), rather than purely as a stand-alone adjective.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 追 relates to moving in pursuit of someone or something
㠯 (yǐ) gives a sound distantly related to 追's reading zhuī, having drifted apart over time
足 (foot) — 踪 names the footprints or tracks left behind.
宗 (zōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 踪.

example.hanzi: 警方正在追踪嫌疑人的行踪。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng zhèngzài zhuīzōng xiányírén de xíngzōng.
example.english: Police are tracking the suspect's whereabouts.
example.fact: 追踪 combines 追 ("to chase, pursue") with 踪 ("footprint, trace") — a vivid image of following the marks something leaves behind, which is likely why the word extended naturally to the modern tech sense of "to track" a shipment or, in Hong Kong/Taiwan usage, "to follow" someone on social media.

components.note: 心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.

example.hanzi: 听到这个消息,她非常伤心。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào zhège xiāoxi, tā fēicháng shāngxīn.
example.english: Hearing this news, she was very heartbroken.
example.fact: 伤心 is a verb-object compound built from 伤 ("to wound, injure") plus 心 ("heart") — literally "to wound the heart." It belongs to a large family of Chinese emotion words that locate feeling physically in the heart, alongside 心疼 ("to feel for/love dearly") and 开心 ("happy," literally "to open the heart").

components.note: 母 (mǔ, 'mother') serves as the phonetic base; the sound has since diverged from měi, so the connection is mostly historical today.
冫 (originally a mark for repetition, unrelated to its later meaning 'ice') — suggests something done more than once.
欠 (a person yawning, mouth open) — repeated yawning gave 次 its meaning of a 'time' or occurrence, as in counting how many times something happens.

example.hanzi: 每次见到她,我都很开心。
example.pinyin: Měicì jiàndào tā, wǒ dōu hěn kāixīn.
example.english: Every time I see her, I'm happy.
example.fact: 每次 almost always pairs with a later 都 (每次...都..., "every time... without exception") — a fixed two-part pattern that Chinese keeps in full even in cases where English would consider one half redundant.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 报 relates to taking action against someone.
卩 (a kneeling or bound person) — handling a wrongdoer and announcing the judgment gave 报 its meaning 'to report' or 'to announce.'
纟 (silk/thread) — early paper was made from silk and plant fibers, linking 纸 to the thread radical.
氏 (shì) gives a sound distantly related to zhǐ, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Yéye měitiān dōu kàn bàozhǐ.
example.english: Grandpa reads the newspaper every day.
example.fact: 报纸 literally means "report paper" (报 "to report, announce" + 纸 "paper") — a plainly descriptive compound naming exactly what the object is: the paper that carries the reports.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 机 originally referred to a wooden device or machine, such as a loom.
几 depicts a small table or stool — combined with 木 (wood), the character pictured a wooden machine or mechanism.
口 (a vessel), shown four times — a set of cooking vessels.
犬 (a dog) — guarding the vessels, the source of 器's meaning 'vessel, tool, instrument.'

example.pinyin: Zhè tái jīqì huài le.
example.english: This machine is broken.
example.fact: 机 alone already means "machine, mechanism" (手机 "cell phone," 飞机 "airplane"), and 器 alone means "tool, vessel, instrument" — 机器 pairs two already machine-adjacent characters into one general word, the same reinforcing strategy behind 喜欢 and 应该 in the character deck's early ranks.

components.note: 角 (horn) — 解 pictures removing a part of an animal.
牛 (ox) — together with a knife cutting between horn and ox, 解 pictures separating something into parts, giving its meaning 'to untie' or 'to explain.'
Bird — an older semantic root kept from an earlier character shape.
Gives the sound hù, related to gù but drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 公司上个月解雇了几名员工。
example.pinyin: Gōngsī shàng gè yuè jiěgùle jǐ míng yuángōng.
example.english: The company laid off several employees last month.
example.fact: 解雇 sits at a formal, HR/legal register; everyday spoken Chinese more often reaches for the blunter 开除 ("to expel, fire," with a punitive tone) or the slang 炒 (from 炒鱿鱼, literally "to fry squid") — three different registers for describing the same event of losing a job.

components.note: 页 (from 頁, head) relates 颜 to the face, part of the head.
彦 (yàn) gives a sound close to yán, differing mainly in tone.
⺈ (a person, bent over) — the figure whose outward expression is being depicted.
巴 — traditionally linked to desire or emotion, so together the character points to a person's expression or complexion, extended to 色's meaning 'color, appearance.'

example.pinyin: Nǐ zuì xǐhuan shénme yánsè?
example.english: What color do you like best?
example.fact: 颜色 combines 颜 ("face, countenance") with 色 ("color, complexion") — before settling into its modern neutral sense of "color," the compound's roots pointed to reading someone's expression. That older link survives in the menacing idiom 给你点颜色看看 ("I'll show you," literally "give you a bit of color to look at").

components.note: 女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'
艹 (grass) — 莱 names a weedy plant, goosefoot.
来 (lái) is an exact match for the sound of 莱.
土 (earth, soil) — 坞 (a dock, an embankment) is an earthen structure.
乌 (wū) gives a sound close to wù, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 这部电影是好莱坞大片。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng shì Hǎoláiwù dàpiàn.
example.english: This movie is a big Hollywood blockbuster.
example.fact: 好莱坞 is a phonetic transliteration of "Hollywood," with characters chosen to approximate the English sound (hǎo-lái-wù) rather than for their literal meanings ("good," "come," "dock") — the same naming strategy used for 墨西哥, also in this batch.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì gēn wǒ wúguān.
example.english: This matter has nothing to do with me.
example.fact: 无关 typically completes the frame 跟/与 + noun + 无关 ("unrelated to ___") rather than standing as a free adjective — 与...无关 favors written or legal register, while 跟...无关, as used here, is the everyday spoken version.

components.note: 日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form
儿 (a person) — shown carrying a torch overhead, the source of 光's meaning 'light, brightness.'
火 (fire) — the torch's flame, the thing giving off the light.

example.hanzi: 童年的时光一去不复返。
example.pinyin: Tóngnián de shíguāng yí qù bú fù fǎn.
example.english: The time of childhood is gone and will never return.
example.fact: 时光 carries a more poetic, wistful flavor than the neutral, everyday 时间 — 时间 works fine for "what time is it" or "I don't have time," but 时光 turns up in reflective or nostalgic writing about time slipping away, closer to English "the sands of time" than to a clock reading.

components.note: 讠 (speech/writing) — the act of putting words down.
己 (oneself, private) — writing down one's own private notes or memories, giving 记 its meaning 'to record, remember.'

example.hanzi: 这位记者采访了很多名人。
example.pinyin: Zhè wèi jìzhě cǎifǎngle hěn duō míngrén.
example.english: This reporter has interviewed many celebrities.
example.fact: 者 as a suffix turns a verb into "one who does X" — 记 ("to record") plus 者 gives "one who records," the same pattern behind 读者 ("reader"), 作者 ("author"), and 学者 ("scholar").

components.note: 忄 (heart/mind) — the state of mind being described.
夬 (a decisive, resolute action) — a resolute state of mind, giving 快 its meaning 'fast, quick.'

example.pinyin: Qǐng jǐnkuài huífù wǒ de yóujiàn.
example.english: Please reply to my email as quickly as possible.
example.fact: 尽 in 尽快 is read jǐn ("to the greatest extent"), a different tone from the more familiar jìn in 尽力 ("to exhaust one's strength, try one's best") — the same character, two tones, and two related but distinct shades of meaning that often trip up learners who default to the more common jìn reading.

components.note: 介 (jiè) gives a sound hint — 价 is pronounced jià, sharing the same initial consonant though the vowel has shifted.
亻 (person) — 值 relates to worth or value assigned by a person
直 (zhí) gives the sound — 值 is also pronounced zhí, an exact match

example.pinyin: Zhè fú huà hěn yǒu jiàzhí.
example.english: This painting is very valuable.
example.fact: 价值 usually shows up inside the set phrase 有价值 ("to have value," i.e. "valuable") rather than as a stand-alone adjective directly modifying a noun — to simply say something "is valuable," Chinese leans on 有价值 or the adjective 珍贵.

components.note: 亻 (person) on the left represents someone tending to something small.
子 (child) on the right depicts the small, young thing being watched over, giving 仔 its meaning of something small or young.
纟 (silk/thread) — 细 relates to something as fine and thin as silk thread
田 (tián) gives a loose sound connection to 细's reading xì

example.pinyin: Qǐng zǐxì jiǎnchá zhè fèn hétong.
example.english: Please carefully check this contract.
example.fact: In 仔细, 仔 keeps its literary reading zǐ (rather than the colloquial zǎi heard in words like 仔仔, "kid"). 仔细 itself pairs naturally with verbs of perception and inspection (仔细看, 仔细听, 仔细检查) to mean "carefully, attentively," while its near-synonym 小心 leans toward physical caution around danger (小心台阶, "watch the steps") — a split between mental attentiveness and physical wariness that English "careful" doesn't separate.

components.note: 工 (work, tool) — 巧 relates to skill in craft or work.
丂 (kǎo) gives a sound close to qiǎo.
十 (here representing a weapon or armor) — 克 pictures overcoming an opponent.
兄 (a person, here representing a formidable figure) — overcoming a strong opponent gave 克 its meaning 'to overcome' or 'to be able to.'
力 depicts the blade of a plow — since plowing fields took great physical effort, the shape came to represent strength or power.

example.pinyin: Tā zuì ài chī qiǎokèlì dàngāo.
example.english: She loves eating chocolate cake most.
example.fact: 巧克力 is a phonetic loanword transliterating English "chocolate," with each character chosen for sound rather than sense — 巧 ("clever"), 克 ("gram; to overcome"), 力 ("strength") add up to no coherent meaning at all, unlike a calque such as 电脑 ("electric brain" = computer) that translates the concept piece by piece.

components.note: 女 depicts a kneeling figure with arms crossed, a traditional posture — a simple picture of a woman.
屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.

example.pinyin: Bān lǐ yǒu shí gè nǚshēng.
example.english: There are ten girls in the class.
example.fact: 女生 literally frames someone by their status as a student (女 "female" + 生 "student, pupil," the same 生 as in 学生) — in casual speech it has broadened to mean simply "girl/young woman" even outside school, paralleling how 男生 ("male student") loosened into a general word for "guy."

components.note: 互 depicts two hooked or interlocking shapes, holding onto each other to show mutual connection.
木 (tree) — 相 pictures looking closely at a tree.
目 (eye) — staring closely at a tree to examine it gave 相 the meaning 'to observe' or, later, 'each other, mutual.'

example.pinyin: Wǒmen yīnggāi hùxiāng bāngzhù.
example.english: We should help each other.
example.fact: 互相 is an adverb placed directly before the verb (互相帮助, "help each other") rather than after it the way English places "each other" — a word-order mismatch that often causes learners to misplace it in the sentence.

components.note: 厂 (a building/shelter) — 厕 relates to a structure.
则 (zé) gives a sound distantly related to 厕's reading cè, having drifted apart over time.
户 (door) — 所 evokes a location or place, such as where a door stands.
斤 (axe) — combined with 户 (door), the image of an axe at a door gave rise to the abstract sense of 'a place' or 'that which.'

example.pinyin: Qǐngwèn, cèsuǒ zài nǎlǐ?
example.english: Excuse me, where is the restroom?
example.fact: 厕所 is the neutral, everyday word for "toilet/restroom"; more indirect terms like 洗手间 ("hand-washing room") or 卫生间 ("hygiene room") are often preferred in polite or formal settings, much as English speakers might ask for the "restroom" rather than name the fixture directly.

components.note: 辛 (bitter, suffering) — 辜 relates to wrongdoing and its consequences.
古 (gǔ) gives a sound close to gū, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 很多无辜的人在这场灾难中受伤。
example.pinyin: Hěn duō wúgū de rén zài zhè chǎng zāinàn zhōng shòushāng.
example.english: Many innocent people were injured in this disaster.
example.fact: 无辜 describes freedom from wrongdoing or blame in a serious, often legal or moral context (无辜的受害者, "an innocent victim") — for the lighter, everyday sense of "innocent" as in a child's unworldly look, Chinese instead reaches for 天真 ("naive, innocent").

components.note: 切 (to cut) — 彻 describes something carried through completely, as if cutting all the way through.
彳 (chì) gives a sound close to chè.
广 (a building/shelter) — 底 relates to the base or bottom, as of a structure
氐 (dǐ) gives the sound — 底 is also pronounced dǐ, an exact match

example.pinyin: Zhè cì gǎigé fēicháng chèdǐ.
example.english: This reform is very thorough.
example.fact: 彻底 can sit on either side of the verb it modifies — before it as an adverb (彻底解决, "resolve thoroughly") or after 得 as a complement (解决得彻底, "resolved thoroughly") — letting the same word describe how completely an action was carried out from either position.

components.note: 辶 (to walk/move) — shows 过's core meaning of 'passing through' or 'crossing'
咼 (guō) gives a sound close to 过's reading guò; the simplified form 过 now uses 寸 in place of 咼, but the phonetic connection traces back to the traditional character 過
禾 (grain) — 程 originally named a unit for measuring grain, extended to 'process, journey, degree.'
呈 (chéng) gives the sound — 程 is also pronounced chéng, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 学习语言是一个漫长的过程。
example.pinyin: Xuéxí yǔyán shì yí gè màncháng de guòchéng.
example.english: Learning a language is a long process.
example.fact: 过程 combines 过 ("to pass through, cross") with 程 ("a measured stage, journey") — its image of "the stages passed through" lines up closely with English "process," itself from Latin procedere, "to go forward": two unrelated languages arriving at a similar journey metaphor for the same abstract idea.

components.note: A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.
冫 (originally a mark for repetition, unrelated to its later meaning 'ice') — suggests something done more than once.
欠 (a person yawning, mouth open) — repeated yawning gave 次 its meaning of a 'time' or occurrence, as in counting how many times something happens.

example.hanzi: 上次我们去的那家餐厅很好吃。
example.pinyin: Shàngcì wǒmen qù de nà jiā cāntīng hěn hǎochī.
example.english: That restaurant we went to last time was delicious.
example.fact: 上次 uses 上 ("up, previous," as in 上个月 "last month") rather than 前 ("before, front") to mark "last/previous" — Chinese consistently treats earlier events as "up" and later ones as "down" (下次, "next time"), the mirror image of English's own "up next."

components.note: The character traces a jagged bolt of lightning splitting the sky, later borrowed for the abstract meaning 'to state, to extend.'
讠 (speech) — relates to 请's meaning 'to request, invite; please,' a spoken request.
青 (qīng) gives a sound hint — 请 is pronounced qǐng, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 我在申请一所大学的研究生项目。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zài shēnqǐng yì suǒ dàxué de yánjiūshēng xiàngmù.
example.english: I'm applying to a university's graduate program.
example.fact: 申请 combines 申 ("to state, extend," from an old pictograph of a lightning bolt) with 请 ("to request") — literally "to formally state a request," a compositional image well suited to its modern bureaucratic sense of filing an application.

components.note: 手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.hanzi: 我手上正拿着一杯咖啡。
example.pinyin: Wǒ shǒu shang zhèng ná zhe yì bēi kāfēi.
example.english: I'm currently holding a cup of coffee in my hand.
example.fact: 手上 extends past its literal sense ("in one's hand") into an idiomatic one meaning "currently in one's possession or charge" (手上的工作, "the work on my plate right now") — much like English "on hand" or "in hand" stretches from a literal grip to a sense of immediate availability or responsibility.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — relates to 请's meaning 'to request, invite; please,' a spoken request.
青 (qīng) gives a sound hint — 请 is pronounced qǐng, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.pinyin: Tā xiàng lǎoshī tíchūle qǐngqiú.
example.english: He made a request to the teacher.
example.fact: 请求 sits at a more formal, deliberate register than the everyday verb 请 ("please, to ask/invite") — 请求 turns up in official, written, or emotionally weighted contexts (请求帮助, "to request help"), while a casual ask usually just uses 请 or 问.

components.note: 圣 is the simplified form of 聖, which combined an ear (耳, listening) and a mouth (口, speaking) above a standing figure — the image of someone who listens and speaks with special insight, giving 圣 its meaning 'holy, sacred.'
讠 (speech) — 诞 originally described boastful, exaggerated speech.
延 (yán) gives a sound distantly related to dàn, having drifted apart over time.
节 is the simplified form of 節, which depicted the segmented sections of a bamboo stalk ⺮ — giving 节 its meaning 'joint, section, festival.'

example.hanzi: 我们全家一起过圣诞节。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen quánjiā yìqǐ guò Shèngdànjié.
example.english: Our whole family celebrates Christmas together.
example.fact: 圣诞节 literally means "holy birth festival" (圣 "holy" + 诞 "birth" + 节 "festival") — a calque translating the Christian meaning of Christmas directly into Chinese, rather than transliterating the English sound the way 巧克力 and 好莱坞 (also in this batch) do.

components.note: 甘 (sweet) — describes the fruit's taste.
木 (tree) — the sweet fruit of an unspecified tree gave 某 its meaning 'a certain, some.'
二 (two) — 些 originally suggested a small plural amount, building on the idea of 'more than one.'
此 (cǐ) is the historical phonetic element; it no longer closely matches the modern reading xiē.

example.hanzi: 某些人对这个消息表示怀疑。
example.pinyin: Mǒuxiē rén duì zhège xiāoxi biǎoshì huáiyí.
example.english: Certain people are skeptical about this news.
example.fact: 某些 deliberately avoids naming who or what is meant — like English "certain people," it hedges in a way that implies the speaker knows specifics but is choosing to withhold them, often to sound diplomatic or quietly pointed.

components.note: A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.
巳 (here representing an eye) — in one traditional theory, this depicted a captive's marked eye, an ancient sign of subjugation, which later broadened to mean 'the common people.'
戈 (a dagger-axe) — combined with the eye shape above, this ties the character to the idea of marking or piercing.

example.hanzi: 人民的生活水平不断提高。
example.pinyin: Rénmín de shēnghuó shuǐpíng búduàn tígāo.
example.english: The people's standard of living keeps improving.
example.fact: 人民 carries a more collective, political register than the plain word 人 ("person/people") — it's the term chosen for a nation's citizenry as a political body, as in 人民共和国 ("People's Republic") and 人民币 ("the people's currency," i.e. RMB), rather than for people as individuals in everyday speech.
